question: Find how teams build it in practice, with concrete settings: OWASP cheat sheets (JSON Web Token, Session Management, HTML5 Security / local storage), identity-provider docs (for example Auth0 / Okta refresh token rotation and reuse detection, Curity token handler, Duende BFF), and framework docs. Must find: the reference architectures (BFF with a session cookie; access token in memory plus refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie; short-lived access token plus a jti denylist), with their real values (token lifetimes, cookie attributes, denylist storage and expiry) and one concrete request/response or configuration example each.

sources.rank_basis: tier B: project's own home (Duende.BFF docs, for facts about Duende.BFF)
tier B: project's own home (Okta developer docs, for facts about Okta's refresh tokens)
tier B: project's own home (dj-rest-auth docs, for facts about configuring dj-rest-auth with SimpleJWT)
tier B: class (curated reference: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series)

facts.summary: The Duende.BFF getting-started host authenticates users with OpenID Connect, keeps the session on the server, and exposes local API endpoints protected against CSRF.
facts.quote: Authenticates users via OpenID Connect and stores the session server-side … Exposes secure local API endpoints with CSRF protection

facts.summary: The BFF 4.0 configuration example uses the code response type, saves tokens in the session, and requests the offline_access scope to receive refresh tokens.
facts.quote: options.ResponseType = "code"; … options.SaveTokens = true; … // Add this scope if you want to receive refresh tokens options.Scope.Add("offline_access");

facts.summary: The example sets the session cookie to SameSite=Lax because the identity provider is on a different site; Strict would keep the cookie from being sent after login. The page recommends Strict when the identity provider is on the same site as the BFF.
facts.quote: Because we use an identity server that's configured on a different site (duendesoftware.com vs localhost), we need to configure the SameSite property to Lax. Setting it to Strict would cause the authentication cookie not to be sent after logging in. … Recommendation: Set it to 'strict' if your IDP is on the same site as your BFF. options.Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax;

facts.summary: The pre-4.0 configuration example names the session cookie with the __Host- prefix ("__Host-blazor").
facts.quote: // Configure the cookie with __Host prefix for maximum security options.Cookie.Name = "__Host-blazor";

facts.summary: Local API routes must be marked with .AsBffApiEndpoint(); without it the X-CSRF header is not enforced and the endpoints are open to CSRF.
facts.quote: It’s important to mark up the APIs with .AsBffApiEndpoint(), because this adds CSRF protection. … Always call .AsBffApiEndpoint() on your local API routes. Without it, the X-CSRF header is not enforced and your endpoints are vulnerable to CSRF attacks.

facts.summary: The frontend checks the session by calling /bff/user with the header X-CSRF: 1; it returns the user's claims as JSON when logged in, or 401/empty when anonymous.
facts.quote: On load, call /bff/user to check whether the user is logged in. This endpoint returns the user’s claims as JSON when authenticated, or a 401/empty response when anonymous. … const response = await fetch('/bff/user', { … headers: { 'X-CSRF': '1' }

facts.summary: Every request to a BFF API endpoint must carry the X-CSRF: 1 header, or the BFF answers 401 Unauthorized.
facts.quote: Every request to a BFF API endpoint must include the X-CSRF: 1 header. Without it, the BFF will reject the request with 401 Unauthorized.

facts.summary: Login and logout are plain links to /bff/login and /bff/logout that trigger a full browser redirect; the logout link must carry the session ID from the logout_url claim.
facts.quote: Use plain anchor tags pointing to the BFF management endpoints. Do not use fetch for these — they must trigger a full browser redirect. … Log in …

facts.summary: Duende.BFF's default server-side session store is in memory, meant for development and testing; sessions are lost on restart.
facts.quote: By default, Duende.BFF uses an in-memory session store. This is suitable for development and testing, but not recommended for production as sessions will be lost when the application restarts.

facts.summary: The in-memory store also cannot be shared across instances; the page says to always use the Entity Framework session store in production.
facts.quote: The default in-memory session store loses all sessions on application restart and cannot be shared across multiple instances. Always use Entity Framework-backed sessions in production.

facts.summary: To notice a session ended on the server side (for example back-channel logout), the frontend can poll /bff/user; the example polls every 60 seconds.
facts.quote: To detect server-initiated session termination (e.g., back-channel logout), poll /bff/user periodically: … // Poll every 60 seconds; redirect to login if session ends

facts.summary: Okta says long-lived refresh tokens are not suitable for SPAs, because a browser has no safe way to store a persistent refresh token for the intended app only.
facts.quote: Long-lived refresh tokens aren't suitable for clients such as single-page apps (SPAs). This is because there isn't a way to safely store persistent refresh tokens in a browser and assure access by only the intended app.

facts.summary: With rotation, Okta invalidates each refresh token once it issues new tokens; if a used refresh token is presented again, Okta invalidates the most recent refresh token and all access tokens issued since the user authenticated.
facts.quote: When the new tokens are issued, Okta invalidates the refresh token that was passed with the initial request to the /token endpoint. … If a previously used refresh token is used again with the token request, the authorization server automatically detects the attempted reuse of the refresh token. As a result, Okta immediately invalidates the most recently issued refresh token and all access tokens issued since the user authenticated.

facts.summary: Okta logs reuse detection as System Log events app.oauth2.as.token.detect_reuse (custom authorization servers) and app.oauth2.token.detect_reuse (org authorization server).
facts.quote: Okta fires the following System Log events when token reuse is detected: app.oauth2.as.token.detect_reuse for custom authorization servers app.oauth2.token.detect_reuse for the org authorization server

facts.summary: Okta's grace period keeps the previous refresh token valid for a set time after rotation, for clients on poor networks that never received the new tokens.
facts.quote: when users with poor network connections access apps, new tokens issued by Okta might not reach the client app. … After the refresh token is rotated, the previous token remains valid for the configured amount of time to allow clients to get the new token.

facts.summary: The grace period defaults to 30 seconds and can be set from 0 through 60 seconds.
facts.quote: The default number of seconds for the Grace period for token rotation is set to 30 seconds. You can change the value to any number from 0 through 60 seconds.

facts.summary: Refresh token rotation is Okta's default for SPAs.
facts.quote: Note: Rotating refresh token behavior is the default for SPAs when you create or edit a SPA.

facts.summary: A rotated refresh token has a new value but keeps the expiration date of the first refresh token issued at sign-in.
facts.quote: When a refresh token is rotated, the new refresh_token string in the response has a different value than the previous refresh_token string due to security concerns with single-page apps. However, the expiration date remains the same. The lifetime is inherited from the initial refresh token minted when the user first authenticates.

facts.summary: In the app's settings.oauthClient, the refresh_token object takes rotation_type ROTATE or STATIC and a leeway of 0 through 60; the example is ROTATE with leeway 30.
facts.quote: Accepted values for rotation_type are ROTATE or STATIC. The accepted value for leeway is any number from 0 through 60. "refresh_token": { "rotation_type": "ROTATE", "leeway": 30 }

facts.summary: A leeway of 0 still lets the previous token work until the new token has been generated and returned.
facts.quote: A leeway of 0 doesn't necessarily mean that the previous token is immediately invalidated. The previous token is invalidated after the new token is generated and returned in the response.

facts.summary: Okta's default refresh token lifetime (refreshTokenLifetimeMinutes) is Unlimited, but an unused refresh token expires after seven days; the page asks for a short lifetime with SPAs.
facts.quote: The default value for the refresh token lifetime (refreshTokenLifetimeMinutes) in the actions object (opens new window) is Unlimited. The refresh token lifetime does expire every seven days if it hasn't been used. When you use a refresh token with a SPA, make sure that you keep a short lifetime setting for better security.

facts.summary: Example refresh request: a form POST to /oauth2/v1/token with grant_type=refresh_token, scope=offline_access openid, and the refresh_token value.
facts.quote: http --form POST https://{yourOktaDomain}/oauth2/v1/token \ … grant_type=refresh_token \ redirect_uri=http://localhost:8080 \ scope=offline_access%20openid \ refresh_token=MIOf-U1zQbyfa3MUfJHhvnUqIut9ClH0xjlDXGJAyqo

facts.summary: Example response: a new access token (token_type Bearer, expires_in 3600), an ID token and a refresh token; whether the refresh token is new depends on rotation and the configured lifetime.
facts.quote: If the refresh token is valid, then you get back a new access token, a new ID token, and the refresh token. Whether that refresh token is the same one sent in the request or is a new refresh token depends on: … "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600,

facts.summary: The dj-rest-auth guide presents JWT authentication with HTTP-only cookies as the recommended approach for SPAs.
facts.quote: This guide covers JWT authentication with HTTP-only cookies—the recommended approach for Single Page Applications (SPAs).

facts.summary: Its comparison table lists a token in localStorage or sessionStorage as open to XSS, a token in memory as lost on page refresh, and session cookies as needing CSRF protection.
facts.quote: Token in localStorage | XSS | JavaScript can read and steal tokens | … Token in memory | UX | Lost on page refresh | Session cookies | CSRF | Requires CSRF protection |

facts.summary: Example REST_AUTH settings: access cookie 'access', refresh cookie 'refresh', HttpOnly True, Secure False in development (True in production), SameSite 'Lax'.
facts.quote: REST_AUTH = { 'USE_JWT': True, 'JWT_AUTH_COOKIE': 'access', 'JWT_AUTH_REFRESH_COOKIE': 'refresh', 'JWT_AUTH_HTTPONLY': True, 'JWT_AUTH_SECURE': False, # True in production! 'JWT_AUTH_SAMESITE': 'Lax',

facts.summary: Example SIMPLE_JWT settings: access token lifetime 15 minutes, refresh token lifetime 7 days, refresh token rotation on, and blacklisting after rotation on.
facts.quote: SIMPLE_JWT = { 'ACCESS_TOKEN_LIFETIME': timedelta(minutes=15), 'REFRESH_TOKEN_LIFETIME': timedelta(days=7), 'ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS': True, 'BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION': True,

facts.summary: In the login flow, the API answers POST /login/ by setting HttpOnly cookies for both the access and the refresh token.
facts.quote: SPA->>API: POST /login/ {credentials} API->>JWT: Generate tokens JWT-->>API: access + refresh tokens API-->>Browser: Set HttpOnly cookies for access and refresh

facts.summary: When the access cookie has expired, the API returns 401; the SPA then calls POST /token/refresh/ with the refresh cookie and receives a new access cookie.
facts.quote: API-->>Browser: 401 Unauthorized SPA->>API: POST /token/refresh/ with refresh cookie API->>JWT: Validate refresh, generate new access JWT-->>API: New access token API-->>Browser: Set new access cookie

facts.summary: With JWT_AUTH_HTTPONLY True the cookies cannot be read by JavaScript and the refresh token is left out of the JSON response; with False the tokens are readable by JavaScript and returned in the body.
facts.quote: When True: - Cookies cannot be accessed via JavaScript (document.cookie) - Protects against XSS attacks - Refresh token is NOT included in JSON response (only in cookie) When False: - Tokens are accessible via JavaScript - Tokens are included in JSON response body

facts.summary: JWT_AUTH_SECURE must be True in production; False is only for local development without HTTPS.
facts.quote: Always set JWT_AUTH_SECURE = True in production. The only reason to set it to False is for local development without HTTPS.

facts.summary: JWT_AUTH_SAMESITE defaults to 'Lax', which the guide recommends; 'Strict' is the most secure but may break some flows, and 'None' requires Secure.
facts.quote: 'JWT_AUTH_SAMESITE': 'Lax', # Default, recommended … 'Strict' | Only same-site requests | Maximum security, may break some flows | … 'None' | All requests (requires Secure) |

facts.summary: Logout invalidation uses SimpleJWT's token_blacklist app, added to INSTALLED_APPS and created with a migration.
facts.quote: Enable token blacklisting to invalidate tokens on logout: … 'rest_framework_simplejwt.token_blacklist', … python manage.py migrate

facts.summary: With ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS and BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION on, a user's refresh token is blacklisted at logout and cannot be reused.
facts.quote: 'ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS': True, 'BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION': True, } Now when users logout, their refresh token is blacklisted and cannot be reused.

facts.summary: The security checklist asks for HttpOnly cookies, the token blacklist for logout, and a short access token lifetime of 5 to 15 minutes.
facts.quote: JWT_AUTH_HTTPONLY = True - Prevent XSS … Token blacklist enabled - Proper logout … Short access token lifetime (5-15 minutes)

facts.summary: The production settings example uses Secure True, SameSite 'Lax', an access token lifetime of 5 minutes and a refresh token lifetime of 1 day, with rotation and blacklisting.
facts.quote: 'JWT_AUTH_SECURE': True, 'JWT_AUTH_SAMESITE': 'Lax', } SIMPLE_JWT = { 'ACCESS_TOKEN_LIFETIME': timedelta(minutes=5), 'REFRESH_TOKEN_LIFETIME': timedelta(days=1), 'ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS': True, 'BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION': True,

facts.summary: The proactive refresh strategy schedules the refresh call 1 minute (60000 ms) before the access token's expiration.
facts.quote: // Refresh 1 minute before expiration const refreshTime = accessExpiration.getTime() - Date.now() - 60000;

facts.summary: The OWASP JWT cheat sheet says using a JWT for stateless user sessions is frowned upon.
facts.quote: A JWT is often suggested for “stateless” user sessions. However, this usage is frowned upon.

facts.summary: JWT user sessions need a way to invalidate sessions, such as a deny list of revoked sessions or tokens, which makes them no longer fully stateless; the sheet suggests a plain session system instead.
facts.quote: if you use JWTs for user sessions, you will need a solution for managing session invalidation. This can be achieved using a deny list of revoked sessions/tokens. If your application implements such a deny list, user sessions won't be completely stateless anymore which might defeat the benefits of stateless sessions. You might want to consider using a plain session system

facts.summary: A token consumer may keep a JWT denylist as simple replay protection or as a workaround for invalidating stateless sessions.
facts.quote: In some cases, the consumer of the token might want to maintain a JWT denylist. This might be for example used a simple form of JWT replay protection or as a workaround for the “stateless session” invalidation problem.

facts.summary: The denylist is keyed on the (jti, iss) pair and each entry is inserted with the token's exp as its expiry; the check looks up the same pair.
facts.quote: A JWT deny list can typically be implemented based on the jti and iss claims: def revoke_token(claims): jti = claims.get("jti") iss = claims.get("iss") exp = claims.get("exp") deny_list.insert((jti, iss), exp) … return deny_list.contains((jti, iss))

facts.summary: Keying the denylist on the raw JWT or its SHA-256 hash is unsafe, because a malleable JWT can be re-encoded and bypass the list.
facts.quote: Using the raw JWT or a secure hash of the JWT (SHA-256(token)) as the denylist key is not safe and might expose the application to denylist bypass through JWT malleability.

facts.summary: Before building a denylist, the sheet lists alternatives: a Token Status List, short JWT expiration, and sender-constrained (DPoP or mTLS-bound) access tokens, which limit use of a stolen token but do not prevent its disclosure.
facts.quote: Before implementing such a JWT denylist, you should consider whether there is a better solution for your problem: … Token reuse can be mitigated by using short expiration time in the JWT. Sender-constrained access tokens, such as DPoP-bound tokens or mutual-TLS certificate-bound tokens, limit an attacker's ability to use a stolen token without its associated private key. They do not prevent token disclosure.

facts.summary: For revocation by the issuer, the JWT carries a status claim with the URI of a Token Status List and the token's index in it, and the consumer fetches the list to check revocation.
facts.quote: If revocation of the JWTs by the issuer is needed, the Token Status Lists (TSL) can be used: … the consumer of the token can fetch the TSL to obtain the revocation status of the JWT. The issuer includes a status claim in the JWT. This claims contains the URI of the associated TSL and the index of the status of the JWT within this list:

conflicts.topic: which SameSite value to give the session or token cookie
conflicts.note: Duende recommends Strict when the identity provider is on the same site and uses Lax only for a cross-site one; dj-rest-auth recommends Lax as the default and says Strict may break some flows, with no same-site condition

conflicts.topic: is a JWT a good browser session credential
conflicts.note: OWASP frowns on JWTs for user sessions and points to a plain session system; dj-rest-auth calls JWTs in HTTP-only cookies the recommended approach for SPAs

conflicts.topic: how long an access token should live
conflicts.note: dj-rest-auth's checklist asks for 5 to 15 minutes; Okta's example token response has expires_in 3600 (1 hour), an example value rather than a stated recommendation

conflicts.topic: how long a refresh token held by a browser app may live
conflicts.note: Okta says long-lived refresh tokens do not suit SPAs and asks for a short lifetime; dj-rest-auth's example gives the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie 7 days (1 day in its production example)
